title: Is a Heat Pump Cheaper Than Gas, and Does It Pay for Itself?

narration.licence: commercial: Azure AI Speech terms allow the generated audio in published media

sentences.text: Picture neighbours on the same street who put in heat pumps the same autumn: by February, one has a smaller heating bill and the other a bigger one.
Neither of them is lying.
So is a heat pump actually cheaper to run than a gas furnace, and does it ever pay for itself?

sentences.text: So which wins: the efficiency, or the price?
The arithmetic fits in one line.

Divide the price of electricity by the price of gas, for the same amount of energy, and multiply by the furnace's efficiency: a heat pump whose average efficiency over the season, its seasonal COP, beats that number heats the home for less.

sentences.text: Those are averages, and the rule leaves things out: it ignores time-of-use rates and backup resistance heat, and an average gas price includes the fixed monthly charge, which a home that keeps its gas hookup still pays and one that disconnects saves.

excerpt.doc: EIA, state residential electricity and gas prices
excerpt.text:
Cost of delivered heat ($ per MMBtu of heat): gas furnace = gas $/MMBtu / AFUE; heat pump = electricity $/MMBtu / seasonal COP
  Break-even seasonal COP      = R x AFUE. A heat pump whose seasonal average COP is above this number heats more cheaply than
  the furnace at these average prices (ignores tiered or time-of-use rates, and backup resistance heat).
Caveat: EIA average prices are total revenue divided by volume, so they include fixed monthly customer charges. A household that keeps its gas
  connection for other appliances keeps paying the fixed charge, and its marginal gas price is below the average; one that disconnects saves it.
Prices used: 2024 annual electricity with 2024 annual gas (same year). "Latest" uses Jan-Jul 2026 YTD electricity with 2025 annual gas.

Example (U.S.): electricity 2024 = 16.48 c/kWh -> 16.48 x 293.07 / 100 = $48.30/MMBtu; gas 2024 = $14.50/Mcf -> 14.50 / 1.036 = $14.00/MMBtu;
  R = 48.30 / 14.00 = 3.45; break-even COP at AFUE 0.95 = 3.45 x 0.95 = 3.28; at AFUE 0.80 = 2.76.
excerpt.highlight: they include fixed monthly customer charges

sentences.text: What happens in real homes?

In Britain, a study of homes that replaced a gas boiler with a heat pump found their total energy use fell by 40 percent, yet because electricity costs more per kilowatt-hour than gas, the running costs came out slightly higher.

sentences.text: The same working paper then looked at Cosy, Octopus's own tariff that prices electricity by the time of day, and estimated that customers who switched to it saved money against Octopus's standard tariff, most of it from shifting their use into cheaper hours.

excerpt.doc: Bernard 2024 (NBER), UK heat pumps and a time-of-use tariff
excerpt.text:
The impacts of Cosy result in near-zero impacts on CO2eq abatement and large reductions
in customers’ annual expenditure on energy. Switching to Cosy saves customers £318 per year
compared to if they were on the standard tariff at Octopus Energy. This is 17.9% of their pre-Cosy
adoption electricity bill, assuming they were on Octopus Energy’s standard non-time-of-use
tariff. Of this £318 in savings, £78 is “structural” winnings (customers would save £78 per year
even if their consumption patterns did not change), while £240 comes from their annualized
consumption changes by period, multiplied by the difference in marginal price between the
Cosy tariff and Octopus Energy’s standard tariff, for each period of the day. Assuming these
figures persist across 20 years, the net present value of these savings is £4,675.67

sentences.text: In the US, an RMI model of Houston found a tariff is not enough by itself: a standard heat pump on a free-nights plan cost more than on a flat rate, and only one controlled to heat and cool ahead while power was free saved, around $1,000 in net present cost.

Heat pump systems on TXU Energy’s “Free Nights” rate, with higher electricity prices during the day
and free electricity at nights, have higher costs than heat pumps on a flat rate plan, due to the
significant

daytime cooling load in Houston. However, for a customer who does use the Free Nights rate,
optimizing heat pumps for demand flexibility saves around $1,000 in net present cost. This includes
preheating water overnight and precooling or preheating the home aggressively while electricity is
free to reduce consumption during the day.

sentences.text: So is a heat pump cheaper to run than gas? For a gas home that already has air conditioning and gets a well-performing heat pump, the national model says it usually is; with a weaker unit, it often is not, and the more your electricity costs next to your gas, the better the heat pump has to be.

sentences.text: Which brings us to when you buy.

A Minnesota study priced a cold-climate heat pump with a propane furnace as backup at $9,450 installed: with nothing broken, that whole price was the extra cost, and the payback ran to well over a decade, depending on the furnace it was compared with.

When the air conditioner alone had failed, the payback roughly halved, and when the furnace and the air conditioner both needed replacing, the extra cost fell to $370 and the payback to about a year or less.

For a gas home whose furnace still works, the evidence says it rarely does on energy savings alone; bought when the furnace and the air conditioner both need replacing, or when the home is adding cooling anyway, the extra cost can shrink to little or nothing, while with only the air conditioner due it shrinks but does not vanish.
